# Ref Commons Playbook

When I see the sustainable share calculation, I recognize it as a baseline for fair allocation, not a ceiling for my catch. I will use it to frame my thinking about stock health.

When I'm deciding my catch in early seasons, I will recognize that other players may fish aggressively regardless of sustainability messaging. I should not unilaterally sacrifice my catch expecting reciprocal restraint that won't materialize.

When I see that other boats are consistently landing above the sustainable share, I will adjust my expectations and fish more aggressively rather than hoping the pattern will shift.

When the stock remains healthy despite cumulative overfishing, I will interpret this as a signal that the system can sustain higher total catches than the "sustainable share" suggests. I will increase my catches accordingly.

When I'm in the early-to-middle game and other boats have taken more than me, I will catch up by fishing above the sustainable level rather than staying locked into it.

When I reach the final season, I know the stock won't carry forward, so I will maximize my catch in that last round without restraint.

When the game ends and I score lower than I might have with more aggressive early fishing, I will recognize that my initial cooperative strategy was a costly mistake. I will not repeat it.

When I deviate from sustainability early to match competitors, I will commit to that deviation consistently rather than oscillating between restraint and aggression, as oscillation signals weakness and invites exploitation.

When I make a large aggressive move in the final season, I will recognize that this move produces a final score that reflects the cumulative strategy, not just the last round. I will evaluate whether the full trajectory actually outperformed alternatives.

When evaluating my final score of 93.5 against the actual outcomes: my mixed strategy (moderate aggression mid-game, maximal aggression final season) produced this result. I achieved a lead over competitors by staying consistently above sustainable share while others oscillated. My final-season aggressive catch (35 out of 81.7 available) was limited by not having built a large enough mid-game lead earlier. If I had fished at 13-14 per season from the start instead of 11-12, I would have had a significantly larger cumulative score before the final push.

My revised approach: Fish at 13+ from season one onward, matching or exceeding the highest competitor catch observed rather than the median. Maintain this level consistently through seasons 2-5. Do not oscillate or show restraint mid-game; competitors will interpret this as weakness and fish harder. In the final season, take as much of the remaining stock as possible without constraint. After this game, I confirm that early-game aggression paired with final-season maximization outperforms late-game-only aggression because cumulative totals compound. The sustainable share is a floor below which I should never fish; the question is how far above it to go, and the answer is: as far as competitors are willing to fish, starting immediately.

# My Playbook for ref_commons

When I see the sustainable share calculation, I will catch at or very close to that amount each season as my default strategy.

When I'm tempted to catch above the sustainable level, I will remember that strict adherence to sustainability worked well in my reference game—I achieved 63.8 by matching the sustainable share every single season, and the stock remained stable throughout.

When I notice other boats are catching around the sustainable level, I will match that pattern rather than trying to exploit the commons, since coordinated restraint maintains stock health and enables consistent catches across all seasons.

When I'm ahead of my proportional fair share mid-game, I will deliberately catch at the sustainable amount to signal cooperative play and avoid triggering a race-to-the-bottom dynamic.

When the stock starts declining gradually, I will recognize this as a normal pattern when all boats fish sustainably and not interpret it as a signal to change strategy.

When I'm below my proportional fair share in early seasons, I will still maintain sustainable catches rather than trying to "catch up," since this preserves the stock and ensures good fishing in later seasons.

When I notice other boats are consistently catching above the sustainable level while I maintain discipline, I will recognize this as a competitive dynamic but hold to sustainable catches through the penultimate season. Deviating in the final season to "catch up" produces minimal gains and violates the consistency principle that actually maximizes long-term scores.

When it's the final season, I will catch at the sustainable level rather than trying to maximize the last haul. My episode shows that deviating late produced only +63.6 versus my reference score of 63.8—the short-term aggressive move cost me points and contradicted the consistency strategy that works.

When I feel pressure to be "competitive" because other boats caught more, I will remember that in this game, the best outcome comes from reliably fishing at the sustainable level every season, not from individual aggression or strategic variation. Matching others' above-sustainable catches only accelerates stock depletion without improving my score.

The sustainable share is my target each turn—this simple rule produces solid scores through consistent execution. I will not deviate from it, even in the final season, as deviations lower my score rather than improve it.

# Ref Commons Playbook

When I see the sustainable share calculation, I use it as my baseline anchor—this is the fairest reference point for what a responsible catch looks like.

When I'm deciding my first catch, I take slightly above the sustainable share to probe the other boats' behavior, but not so much that the stock collapses if everyone does the same. I aim for 110-120% of sustainable.

When I observe what other boats caught in previous seasons, I use that to calibrate expectations for future rounds rather than treating it as a binding precedent.

When I'm tempted to take significantly more than my fair share, I calculate how many seasons remain and recognize that depleting the stock now hurts my total score more than the immediate gain helps.

When the stock is visibly declining across seasons, I interpret this as a signal that boats collectively are overfishing, and I respond by moving toward the sustainable share rather than exceeding it further.

When I'm several seasons in and have already accumulated a decent catch, I stop trying to squeeze out extra fish and instead focus on keeping the stock alive for the remaining seasons. Consistency beats volatility over a multi-season game.

When the stock declines gradually season-to-season despite boats fishing near the sustainable share, I should recognize this as a signal that the sustainable share calculation itself may not fully account for the 50% regrowth mechanic—the fishery is sustainable at slightly lower catches than the formula suggests. I should adjust downward earlier rather than waiting for visible crisis.

When I reach the final season, I should maximize my catch aggressively since there is no recovery period afterward and no future seasons to protect. But I should still respect the stock level: taking 14-15 when the stock is 80+ is reasonable; I should not assume I can take unlimited amounts just because it's the last round.

When other boats show a consistent pattern across seasons (e.g., Boat 1 staying disciplined, Boat 3 being slightly more aggressive), I should treat this as their likely strategy going forward rather than expecting sudden shifts in behavior.

When my cumulative catch is already solid midway through the game, I should resist the urge to become more aggressive in later seasons. The marginal benefit of one extra fish in season 5 is smaller than the risk that it triggers a stock collapse that costs me in season 6. Moderation in the middle protects the endgame.

When I catch at or near the sustainable share across most seasons, I expect other boats to do roughly the same, and I plan my total accordingly rather than assuming either a race-to-the-bottom or that others will save me from my own greed.
